extracted.intended_audience: American women, particularly housewives and domestic readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical moral and social guidance for women in domestic and public life, covering speech, discretion, treatment of servants, nervousness, and methods for cultivating agreeable personal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uttering bitter or harsh words
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave the bitter word unspoken; do not 'give the piece of your mind' or utter cruel sentences that cannot be recalled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sentence once uttered is gone forever and may leave a lasting scar even if forgiveness follows. Refrain from sharp retorts and 'the barbed arrows of our eloquence'—they often only make others hate you and do not change their behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice restraint: repress harsh answers, confess faults, stop in self-defence
rubrics_metrics.description: To repress a harsh answer, to confess a fault, to stop, right or wrong, in the midst of self-defence, in gentle submission, sometimes requires a struggle like life and death, but these three efforts are the golden threads with which domestic happiness is woven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate self-restraint and occasional quiet confession are framed as central duties for preserving domestic harmony; these are active practices, not passive concessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer kindness or silence over uncharitable remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot say a kind thing say nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncharitable remarks and wholesale criticism. When discussing someone's virtues, do not spoil it by pointing out a minor defect ('it is such a pity that she does not read more'). Wholesale criticism is easy to form and grows rapidly—cultivate saying nothing rather than unkindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gossip and scandal-mongering
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of the gossip is so thankless that it is a marvel any one accepts it; the gossip delights in relating scandal and often manufactures material if none exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gossips not only harm their subjects but will carry ugly stories about you in turn. Do not give undue attention to 'choice bits of scandal' or follow imaginary clues; refrain from being the first to relate unsavory tales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard confidences; limit the number of confidantes
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a secret and wish to keep it, guard it jealously. It ceases to be yours alone when you impart it to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is comfort in unburdening to a trusted friend, but draw a line: too many confidantes increases risk. Even a seemingly discreet confidante may share with someone who 'tells everything'. You may regret what you have told more than what you have kept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let others be mistaken on unimportant matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the hardest struggle is to let others be mistaken. Why antagonize a man by correcting an unimportant error?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not correct trivial inaccuracies (dates, story details) that are unimportant; correcting them needlessly may antagonize and gain nothing. Ask whether the correction benefits anyone before speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not remind people of past opinions they've changed
rubrics_metrics.description: Never tell one of an opinion which he once held, if he has since had reason to alter his views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no sin in changing one's mind; reminding someone of past statements that they have since revised causes shame and resentment. Avoid bringing up earlier mistakes of opinion—'there is no more bitter diet than to be forced to eat one's own words.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be truthful and fair when writing references for servants
rubrics_metrics.description: When dismissing a servant, write out without prejudice for or against the late employee, her claims to the confidence of the next employer, and her faults—in short, a veritable 'character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give dishonest, glowing references to avoid trouble; note both positive traits (sober, strong, quick to learn) and faults (wasteful, dirty, ill-tempered). False certificates circulate and harm the system; truthful references help future employers and protect households.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective hiring standards among housekeepers
rubrics_metrics.description: Let each housekeeper pledge not to receive into her family one who cannot produce satisfactory testimonials of her fitness for the place she seeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed remedy: formation of local Housekeepers' Protective Unions with a single article pledging truthful references and refusal to hire without credentials. Such collective self-interest would incentivize skill and fidelity in domestic service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give in to falsehood to avoid social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to give a candid reference may subject you to being boycotted, but yielding to write a false certificate is morally wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh self-interest against duty to neighbors; the author argues to 'stand fast' and be honest even if the social tide says otherwise. Antipathy from other housekeepers is possible, but moral duty and long-term reform favor truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize seriousness of nervous illness and exercise self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no illness more difficult to treat and more trying to bear than nervous prostration; will-power and self-control will do much toward lessening the trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss 'nervousness' as trivial—it's a slowly advancing malady. Distinguish real nervous illness from mere crossness; if physically well, will-power and self-discipline help. The woman who says 'I will be strong' has a better chance of recovery than one who gives way to hysterical sobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaking ordinary crossness for nervousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself 'Are we nervous, or cross?' If the latter, remedy it; a well person has no right to be abominably bad-tempered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before excusing bad temper as 'nerves,' consider practical causes (poor sleep, dyspepsia) and correctable behaviors. Self-control improves physical and social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help sufferers with compassion and recognize their strength
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not know what nervousness is, pity and help the poor sufferer in your family who never knows what it is to be without 'the fussiness that sets you wild.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate self-control in sufferers who manage their condition; the one who curbs impulses is to be commended rather than mocked. Offer support rather than scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively cultivate friendship by first liking others and finding their good traits
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher's answer—'Because she loves the lamb'—is applied: 'The most laudatory speech failed to make my heart glow as warmly as the remark of an old friend... you always were, and still are, my affinity.' 'Because she is first attracted by them'—she goes on the principle that there is some good in everybody and sets herself to find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be the first to find and acknowledge others' good qualities; offer delicate compliments rather than fulsome flattery. Making the best of everybody is both moral and politic; it increases personal magnetism and social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone down eccentricities and avoid pride in personal defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be proud of personal defects and peculiarities; they are subjects for regret, not pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pronounced personal 'colors' out of strong light; shade them so they form harmonious combinations with others. If you boast 'I know I am often impatient,' you acknowledge a weakness you should correct—consider staying apart until self-control is learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: When genuine, uncontrollable antipathy exists, avoid but do not publicize it
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the first there is a strong, uncontrollable personal antipathy, avoid him; it is not necessary to tell others of the uncomfortable impression he has made upon you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some rare characters will repel you physically and mentally; discretion is to avoid contact rather than to broadcast dislike. For ordinary dislikes, analyze their cause—often wounded self-esteem—and quench the spark before it ignites enmity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make an effort to be interesting and not selfishly bored
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people are always bored; they look at everything from a selfish standpoint and ask 'How does that affect me?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you feel bored with a conversation, consider whether the other person is simply not talking about your interests. Make the effort to turn discussion toward their interests or find something in them to be curious about—being entertaining often requires effort, not complaint.
